t3sd-rankings: Short-deck starting-hand strength differs fundamentally from standard hold'em, from two rule changes: (1) hand-ranking reshuffle — trips > straights, flushes > full houses; (2) pair density — pocket pairs rise from 5.9% to 8.6% of starting hands. Result: pocket pairs rise in value (easier to make trips, and trips is one of the strongest made hands), while big high-card hands like AK shift subtly in relative value.

Short-deck starting-hand rule: AA/KK remain top tier; AK is the "strongest non-pair", roughly a coin flip or better against small-mid pocket pairs preflop all-in; pocket pairs stand on their made-hand strength after flopping trips (about 17.1%).
AK vs Pocket Pairs in Short Deck

Short-deck AK vs pocket-pair preflop all-in comparison (36-card deck, exact-enumeration magnitudes):

AK vs small-mid pocket pairs (66-QQ): about 50%-56% (coin flip or better; AKs vs QQ ≈ 53.7%, AKo vs QQ ≈ 51.8%)
AK vs KK: about 32%-35% (KK dominates)
AK vs AA: about 28%-31% (badly behind)
AK vs AK: about 50% (mostly split pots)

Why pocket pairs rise in value:
1. Trips > straights in short deck, so making trips is a very strong hand
2. High pair density means flopping trips is more likely (about 17.1%)
3. Full-ring AK trails small pairs; short deck inverts it to slightly ahead — pairs lose their preflop equity edge and stand on made-hand strength after trips

AK's value: still the strongest hand dominating other non-pairs, and it can flop top pair postflop. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker starting-hand strength and 6+ rules; equities are exact-enumeration magnitudes)

Practical meaning of the short-deck reshuffle: preflop all-in, AK is roughly a coin flip or better against small-mid pocket pairs — short deck's "flip" runs opposite to full ring (where AK slightly trails small pairs). Meanwhile, suited connectors (JTs, 98s) are playable because straights/flushes are valuable, but they belong to a secondary tier — they can win big pots (make nuts) yet are weaker preflop than pairs and AK.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ and the opponent 3-bets all-in preflop. Your hand is the "strongest non-pair"; against a small-mid pocket pair (e.g. 88) you have about 50%-55% (slightly ahead), but a range containing AA/KK dominates you. The decision depends on pot odds and the opponent's range: if the range is mostly small-mid pairs and you need only ~45%, call is +EV; with lots of AA/KK, fold carefully. The key is short-deck-corrected equity (AK slightly ahead of small-mid pairs, behind AA/KK), not one full-ring intuition.

Example 2 (small-pair value): Short deck, you hold 7♠7♦ facing a raise preflop. In short deck 77 flops trips about 17.1% of the time (full ring 12%), and trips is a strong made hand (only loses to full houses/flushes). So small pairs (66-99) rise significantly in short-deck value — set mining still needs a higher threshold (T2), but the strength and frequency of made trips both support more calls.

Counterintuitive point: "AK is strong" in short deck needs the right reading. AK dominates all non-pairs and can flop top pair; it's roughly a coin flip or better against small-mid pairs and trails only AA/KK badly. Transplanting the full-ring memory "AK trails pairs" into short deck misjudges AK's preflop value.

Short-deck starting-hand quick memory: AA/KK top tier, other pairs next (trips value), AK strongest non-pair, suited connectors (JTs+) playable but secondary. For preflop all-ins, AK vs small-mid pairs is a slight favorite while pairs vs AA/KK clearly trail — drop both full-ring intuitions.
t3sd-suitedness: Short Deck: The Rise of Flushes

In short deck, a flush beats a full house — the fundamental difference from standard hold'em (where full house > flush). The relative value of flushes rises sharply, making them one of the top made hands in short deck. This changes starting-hand strategy: suited connectors (JTs, 98s, etc.) and suited Ax become significantly more playable — they can make both flushes (nut-tier) and straights.

Short-deck flush rule: flush beats full house — a top-tier made hand. So "suited hands" are worth far more in short deck than in full ring — chasing flush draws has excellent implied odds, and once made they basically lock big pots.

Short-deck suited-connector preflop equity (vs random range):

JTs: about 42%-44%
98s: about 40%-42%
76s: about 38%-40%

Slightly lower than the same hands in full ring (high pair density), but short-deck made-hand value is high:
1. Making a flush (beats full house) → nut-tier
2. Making a straight (connecting across ~8 ranks) → strong hand

Excellent implied odds: chasing flushes/straights deep-stacked pays hugely.

Strategic status: suited connectors are playable but not top tier (AA/KK/QQ/JJ/AK are), so know when to let go against strong preflop resistance. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker flush value and 6+ starting hands)

Suited Ax also rises in short-deck value: A♠K♠, A♠Q♠, etc., can make a flush (beats full house), flop top pair of Aces, and carry an A blocker. But note — suited Ax's value comes from "flush-draw nut potential + top pair", not "AX itself", because short-deck pair density is high and Ax gets dominated by pairs more often.

Example: Short deck, you hold J♠T♠ facing a BTN raise preflop. JTs is playable in short deck: the flop can give a flush draw (high value), a straight draw, or top pair. Though weaker preflop than pairs, its postflop potential is huge. Deep-stacked, actively call or 3-bet-semi-bluff to exploit flush-value implied odds.

Example 2 (flush chase): Short deck, you hold A♥9♥ on a K♥8♦6♣ flop. You draw to the flush (seen A♥9♥K♥ = 3 hearts, flush outs = 9 − 3 = 6). The opponent bets and you call. If the turn brings a heart, your flush is nut-tier (beats full houses) and extracts lots of chips. Short-deck flush draws have few outs (6) but enormous made value — chasing has excellent implied odds.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck suited connectors being "playable" doesn't mean "top-tier strong". They win big pots (making nut flushes/straights) but are weaker preflop than pairs and AK. Treat them as "high-reward speculative hands", not "steady value hands", to use them correctly.

Short-deck flush quick memory: flush beats full house → chasing flush draws is hugely valuable; JTs and above suited connectors are playable; suited Ax has both nut potential and top pair. When facing strong preflop resistance (big 3-bet), suited connectors should let go — they're speculative hands.
t3sd-position: Short-deck position value is amplified because draw density is high, decisions are more frequent, and pots are bigger. Being in position (BTN/IP) means you act after seeing the opponent's action, can realize equity more cheaply, and can control pot size. Out of position (BB/OOP) hurts more in short deck — more draws, easier to be outdrawn, and forced into more tough decisions.

Short-deck position rule: with position on the BTN, chase more draws (cheap equity realization); in the BB without position, tighten marginal calls to avoid high-RIO spots. Position in short deck is both an advantage and a risk regulator.
BTN and BB Positional Strategies in Short Deck

BTN (IP) strategy in short deck: open wider and chase draws more aggressively — position lets you realize equity and control pots. BB (OOP) strategy: defend a reasonable range against BTN's wide opens, but pot-control marginal draws (easily outdrawn) to avoid RIO. The core of short-deck OOP play is "pot control + timely stop-loss".

Example: Short deck, you're on the BTN holding 7♠8♠ on a 9♦T♣A♥ flop (open-ended straight draw). IP, betting or calling realizes equity cheaply — make a straight on a 6/J turn, or see a free river/fold when missing. In the BB (OOP) with the same hand, you act first and get squeezed when raised. Position makes the same draw's value completely different.

Example 2 (OOP pot control): Short deck, you're in the BB holding Q♦J♦ on a Q♣9♦8♠ flop (top pair + gutshot). OOP, you act first. Top pair on a wet board has high RIO and you can't realize equity without position. The right play is pot control (small bet or check) — avoid building a big pot then getting outdrawn by straights/flushes. An in-position BTN can instead bet thin value.

Counterintuitive point: out of position in short deck, "aggressively betting to seize the initiative" can backfire. Because draw density is high and you act first OOP, aggression tends to build a big pot and then land in a high-RIO spot. In short deck position is more a "pot control and stop-loss" tool than mindless aggression.

Short-deck position quick memory: BTN/IP → wide opens + aggressive draw chasing (cheap equity realization); BB/OOP → tighten calls + pot control/stop-loss (avoid RIO). Ask "do I have position" for every hand before deciding between aggression and control.
